egg-sandwich-on-white-bread-with-meat.title: Egg and Meat Sandwich on White Bread

content.title: About
content.content: An egg and meat sandwich on white bread is a simple, filling sandwich made with a slice of white bread, a fried egg, and thinly sliced boiled or fried meat (usually ham or chicken). It is popular as a breakfast or quick lunch.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first egg sandwich recipe appeared in the United States in the early 1920s.
White bread is often used for its soft texture that holds the filling well.
The egg provides a complete set of essential amino acids.
Meat adds an extra source of protein and iron.
The sandwich can be easily customized with cheese, vegetables, or sauces.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs and meat together supply high‑quality protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Both egg and meat contain B2, B6, and B12 vitamins that support energy metabolism and the nervous system.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Meat provides heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and carbohydrates from the bread helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Provides vitamin D
items.content: Eggs contain vitamin D, important for bone health and immune function.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Using salty ham or sauces can raise sodium levels, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to eggs, experiencing skin reactions or breathing difficulties.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The sandwich can be calorie‑dense due to butter or oil used for frying the egg and fatty meat.

items.title: Trans‑fat content
items.content: If fried in oil high in trans fats, intake should be limited.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich can be served hot or warm. It is convenient to eat with hands, and you may add lettuce, tomato, or mustard for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sandwich in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours, wrapped in plastic film. For longer storage, keep the components separate.

content.title: About
content.content: Spam is a canned meat product made from pork, beef, salt, sugar, water and sodium nitrite. It was first introduced in 1937 by Hormel Foods and became popular during World War II because of its long shelf life.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first advertising slogan was “It’s the meat you can’t eat without it.”
During the war Spam was supplied to the U.S. military and occupied territories as a reliable protein source.
In Hawaii Spam is a cultural icon; an annual Spam Fest celebrates it.
There are more than 30 flavor variations, including Spicy, Teriyaki and Jalapeño.
In the 2020s Spam has been featured in gourmet restaurant menus.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: One slice of Spam (≈57 g) provides about 7 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nerve function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: High energy density
items.content: Its calorie density makes Spam a convenient energy source in demanding situations.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: A single slice can contain over 800 mg of salt, exceeding daily recommendations for people with hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Spam contains a notable amount of saturated fat, which may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Nitrites used in the recipe can form potentially harmful compounds over long storage periods.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork or beef.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spam can be eaten cold, sliced thin and fried until crisp, added to sandwiches, salads, rice dishes, or used as a filling for omelets.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place. After opening, transfer to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for up to 5 days.
